facts: Algeria is the largest country in Africa, a title it took from Sudan when South Sudan separated in 2011.
About four fifths of its territory is Sahara, so nearly the whole population lives on the northern coastal strip.
The Tassili n'Ajjer plateau holds thousands of prehistoric rock paintings showing a once-green Sahara.
DZ.about: Behind a Mediterranean coastline of nearly 1,000 kilometres, Algeria rises through the folded ridges of the Tell Atlas and the Saharan Atlas before the land opens out into dunes, gravel plains and the volcanic Hoggar massif of the far south. Only the coastal Tell receives reliable winter rain, which is why farming, cities and roads cluster there. France invaded in 1830 and later governed the north as part of France itself, settling a large European population. A war of independence that began in 1954 ended with independence on 5 July 1962, after a conflict that left deep marks on both countries. Oil and natural gas, found mostly in the desert interior, now provide the bulk of export earnings, and pipelines carry Algerian gas under the Mediterranean to Spain and Italy. Arabic is the main language, and Tamazight, the Berber language spoken in Kabylie and other regions, has been an official language since 2016.

facts: Cabinda, Angola's oil-rich province, is an exclave separated from the rest of the country by DR Congo.
Angola is one of Africa's largest oil producers and a significant diamond exporter.
Portuguese is the official language, and Angola has one of the largest Portuguese-speaking populations in Africa.
AO.about: From a narrow, dry coastal plain, Angola climbs steeply to a broad central plateau where most of its farmland and many of its people are found. The cold Benguela Current keeps the southern coast arid, and the Namib Desert reaches across the border from Namibia, while the north and east are wetter savanna and forest drained by rivers such as the Cuanza. Portuguese navigators reached the Congo estuary in the 1480s, and Luanda, founded in 1576, became one of the main ports of the Atlantic slave trade. Independence came on 11 November 1975, but rival liberation movements fought a civil war that lasted, with interruptions, until 2002. Since then reconstruction has been funded largely by oil revenue, though much of the population still depends on small-scale farming. Alongside Portuguese, Bantu languages such as Umbundu, Kimbundu and Kikongo remain widely spoken, reflecting the country's major ethnic groups.

facts: Porto-Novo is the official capital, but Cotonou is the seat of government and the largest city.
The Kingdom of Dahomey, centred here, was known for its all-female military regiment.
Vodun originated in this region and remains an officially recognised religion in Benin.
BJ.about: Long and narrow, Benin stretches more than 600 kilometres inland from a short Atlantic shoreline fringed by lagoons. Lake Nokoué, beside Cotonou, supports the stilt village of Ganvié, where thousands of people live in houses raised above the water. Inland the coastal belt gives way to plateaus and savanna, the Atakora hills rise in the north-west, and the Niger River forms part of the northern border near the Pendjari and W national parks. Under French rule the territory was called Dahomey; it became independent on 1 August 1960 and took the name Benin in 1975. In 1990 a national conference ended military-backed single-party rule, an early example of peaceful democratic transition in Africa. Cotton is the leading agricultural export, and the port of Cotonou handles a large share of goods bound for landlocked Niger. In Ouidah, a memorial gateway on the beach marks the departure point of enslaved Africans shipped across the Atlantic.

facts: The Kalahari covers around 70% of Botswana, a semi-arid sand basin rather than a true desert, and it supports grazing for much of the year.
The Okavango Delta is a rare inland delta, emptying into the desert instead of the sea.
Botswana went from one of the world's poorest countries at independence in 1966 to middle-income status, largely through diamonds.
BW.about: Most of Botswana lies on a flat tableland roughly 1,000 metres above sea level, far from any coast. In the north-east, the Makgadikgadi Pans are among the largest salt flats on Earth, the dry bed of an ancient lake that floods briefly in good rainy seasons and draws great flocks of flamingos. Along the Chobe River in the far north lives one of the largest elephant populations anywhere in Africa. The territory became the British protectorate of Bechuanaland in 1885 and gained independence on 30 September 1966 under Seretse Khama, its first president. Since then it has held regular multiparty elections without interruption, a rare record on the continent. Because the west is so dry, most people live in the east, along the railway corridor close to the South African border. Cattle ranching remains central to rural life and identity, and beef is a long-standing export alongside minerals.

facts: The country's name, adopted in 1984, translates roughly as 'land of upright people'.
It is landlocked and largely flat savanna, with the Sahel across its northern reaches.
FESPACO in Ouagadougou is the largest African film festival on the continent.
BF.about: Three rivers once known as the Black, White and Red Volta drain the gently undulating plateau of Burkina Faso southwards towards Ghana, and they gave the country its colonial name, Upper Volta. Rain falls mainly between June and September, more generously in the south-west than in the north, so farming depends heavily on a single wet season. Long before French rule, the Mossi kingdoms built a centralised state around Ouagadougou, and the Mossi remain the largest ethnic group; their traditional ruler, the Mogho Naba, still holds ceremonial importance. France took control in the 1890s, and the colony became independent on 5 August 1960. Most people farm sorghum, millet and maize for their own needs, while cotton and, increasingly, gold provide export income. The stone ruins of Loropéni in the south-west, linked to the gold trade, were the first site in the country to be inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

facts: Burundi moved its political capital from Bujumbura to Gitega in 2019.
It is one of the most densely populated countries in Africa and among the least urbanised.
Lake Tanganyika on its western border is the second deepest lake in the world.
BI.about: High rolling hills cover much of Burundi, rising in the west to a ridge that divides the Congo and Nile drainage basins; streams on its eastern slopes, including the Ruvyironza, are counted among the most distant headwaters of the Nile. The altitude keeps temperatures mild despite the country's position just south of the Equator. Burundi existed as a kingdom from at least the 17th century, was absorbed into German East Africa in the 1890s and then administered by Belgium with neighbouring Rwanda as Ruanda-Urundi. It became independent as a monarchy on 1 July 1962 and a republic in 1966. Tension between Hutu and Tutsi led to repeated violence and a civil war from 1993 to 2005. Nearly everyone speaks Kirundi, unusual in a region of many languages. Coffee and tea are the main exports, and the ritual dance of the royal drum is listed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.

facts: Cabo Verde is an archipelago of ten volcanic islands about 570 kilometres off the West African coast.
The islands were uninhabited before Portuguese settlement in the 15th century.
More Cabo Verdeans live abroad than in the country itself, and remittances are a major part of the economy.
CV.about: Sitting in the dry belt of the Atlantic, the Cabo Verde islands receive little and unreliable rain, and droughts have caused severe famines in the past. They fall into two groups, the windward Barlavento islands in the north and the leeward Sotavento islands in the south. Fogo is still volcanically active, most recently erupting in 2014–15, while flat, sandy Sal and Boa Vista have become the focus of beach tourism. Portuguese settlers founded Ribeira Grande, now Cidade Velha, on Santiago in 1462, and it grew into an important stopover in the Atlantic slave trade; the old town is a World Heritage Site. Independence came on 5 July 1975 after a liberation struggle waged jointly with Guinea-Bissau. Everyday life is conducted largely in Cape Verdean Creole, and the islands' melancholy morna song tradition, made famous worldwide by Cesária Évora, was added to UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2019.

facts: Cameroon is often called 'Africa in miniature' for containing desert, savanna, rainforest and mountains.
It has both English and French as official languages, a legacy of divided colonial rule.
Mount Cameroon is an active volcano and one of the wettest places on Earth.
CM.about: The country's name comes from the Portuguese Rio dos Camarões, 'river of prawns', given in the 15th century to the Wouri estuary where the port city of Douala now stands. Cameroon stretches from the Gulf of Guinea to a narrow northern tip on Lake Chad, crossing the forested south, the high Adamawa plateau in the centre and the dry savanna of the north. Germany declared the colony of Kamerun in 1884; after the First World War it was divided between France and Britain. French Cameroun became independent on 1 January 1960, and in 1961 the southern part of British Cameroons voted to join it, while the northern part chose Nigeria. Around 250 local languages are spoken, making it one of the most linguistically varied countries in Africa. Oil, cocoa, coffee, cotton and timber are major exports, and Douala's port serves Chad and the Central African Republic as well as Cameroon itself.

facts: The Central African Republic sits almost exactly at the centre of the African landmass.
It is rich in diamonds, gold and uranium yet remains among the world's least developed economies.
Sangha Trinational park, shared with Cameroon and Congo, protects largely undisturbed rainforest.
CF.about: A broad, rolling plateau forms most of the Central African Republic, and it acts as a watershed: rivers in the north flow towards Lake Chad through the Chari system, while those in the south drain into the Ubangi and on to the Congo. Dense forest in the south-west gives way to wooded savanna across the centre and drier Sahelian country in the far north-east. Under French rule the territory was known as Ubangi-Shari, part of French Equatorial Africa, and it became independent on 13 August 1960. From 1976 to 1979 Jean-Bédel Bokassa ruled it as the self-proclaimed Central African Empire. Population is thinly spread and concentrated in the south-west and along the Ubangi, which links the capital by river to Brazzaville. Besides French, Sango serves as a national language and is understood by most of the population, an unusual degree of linguistic unity for the region. Manovo-Gounda St Floris National Park in the north is a World Heritage Site.

facts: Lake Chad has shrunk by roughly 90% since the 1960s through drought and irrigation.
Emi Koussi is a dormant volcano in the Tibesti range, the highest point in the Sahara.
Chad is landlocked, and its capital lies over 1,000 kilometres from the nearest port.
TD.about: Chad spans three broad climate belts: the Saharan north, with the Tibesti mountains and the sandstone Ennedi plateau; a central Sahelian band of grassland and thorn scrub; and a wetter Sudanian south where most farming takes place. The Chari and Logone rivers, which meet at N'Djamena, supply most of the water reaching Lake Chad. In the far north, the Bodélé Depression is thought to be the single largest source of airborne dust on Earth. France brought the territory into French Equatorial Africa in the early 20th century, and it became independent on 11 August 1960, followed by decades of civil conflict between north and south. Arabic and French are both official, and well over 100 local languages are spoken. Since 2003 oil from the southern Doba fields has been exported through a pipeline to the Cameroonian coast. The Ennedi massif and the Lakes of Ounianga, a chain of desert lakes fed by groundwater, are both World Heritage Sites.

facts: The Comoros is a volcanic archipelago between Mozambique and Madagascar.
Mount Karthala has one of the largest active volcanic craters in the world.
It is one of the world's main producers of ylang-ylang, used in perfume.
KM.about: Three main islands make up the Union of the Comoros: Grande Comore (Ngazidja), Mohéli (Mwali) and Anjouan (Ndzuwani). Steep volcanic slopes, thin soils and a humid tropical climate with a cyclone season shape farming, and fishing is important along the coasts. Positioned on Indian Ocean trade routes, the islands absorbed Bantu, Arab, Persian and Malagasy influences over many centuries, and Sunni Islam is almost universal. Comorian, or Shikomori, is closely related to Swahili and is official alongside Arabic and French. France ruled the islands from the 19th century until the Comoros declared independence on 6 July 1975; the fourth island, Mayotte, voted to remain French and is still claimed by the Comoros. The decades after independence saw many coups and attempted coups. Vanilla and cloves are important cash crops, and on Grande Comore the costly 'grand mariage' wedding confers social standing on families.

facts: Brazzaville and Kinshasa face each other across the Congo River, the closest pair of capital cities in the world.
About 60% of the country is rainforest, part of the Congo Basin.
Oil accounts for the large majority of export earnings, most of it pumped offshore near Pointe-Noire.
CG.about: Between a short Atlantic coast and the Congo and Ubangi rivers, the Republic of the Congo crosses several distinct landscapes: a sandy coastal plain, the forested Mayombe escarpment, the fertile Niari valley, the grassy Batéké plateaus, and vast seasonally flooded swamp forests in the north. The capital takes its name from Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza, who signed a treaty with the Teke king Makoko in 1880 that brought the area under French influence. Brazzaville later became the capital of French Equatorial Africa and, in 1940, the symbolic capital of Free France. Independence followed on 15 August 1960, and from 1969 to 1991 the country was a Marxist-Leninist people's republic. Most people live in the south, along the Congo-Ocean Railway linking Brazzaville with the coast. Lingala and Kituba serve as national languages, and Odzala-Kokoua National Park protects large populations of western lowland gorillas and forest elephants.

facts: DR Congo is the second largest country in Africa and holds most of the Congo Basin rainforest.
It produces the majority of the world's cobalt, essential to rechargeable batteries.
The Congo River is the deepest river in the world, exceeding 220 metres in places.
CD.about: Straddling the Equator, the Democratic Republic of the Congo reaches the Atlantic only through a coastline of about 40 kilometres at the mouth of its great river. Its eastern edge follows the Albertine Rift, a chain of deep lakes, including Albert, Edward, Kivu and Tanganyika, overlooked by the Rwenzori mountains and the Virunga volcanoes. Virunga National Park, created in 1925, is the oldest national park in Africa and shelters mountain gorillas. The territory was the personal property of King Leopold II of Belgium as the Congo Free State from 1885, notorious for forced labour, before becoming the Belgian Congo in 1908. Independence came on 30 June 1960; the country was renamed Zaire in 1971 and took its present name in 1997. Hundreds of ethnic groups live here, and Lingala, Swahili, Kikongo and Tshiluba are recognised as national languages. Katanga's copper belt in the south-east has driven mining since the colonial era.

facts: Lake Assal is the lowest point in Africa and one of the saltiest bodies of water on Earth.
Djibouti's position at the Bab-el-Mandeb strait makes it a strategic shipping chokepoint.
It hosts foreign military bases from several countries, more than almost any comparable state.
DJ.about: Djibouti occupies part of the Afar Triangle, one of the few places on land where three tectonic plates are pulling apart, and its landscape of basalt plateaus, salt flats and fault-lined depressions reflects that activity. The Gulf of Tadjoura cuts deep into the country from the east. Summers are extremely hot and rainfall is scarce, so permanent farming is almost impossible and much food is imported. France established a presence in the 1860s and ruled French Somaliland, renamed the French Territory of the Afars and the Issas in 1967, until independence on 27 June 1977. The population is made up mainly of Somali, especially Issa, and Afar communities, and Arabic and French are the official languages. Most people live in the capital, and the economy revolves around its port, which handles the large majority of landlocked Ethiopia's foreign trade via a railway to Addis Ababa. Near Lake Abbe, limestone chimneys vent steam across the plain.

facts: Around 95% of Egyptians live on roughly 5% of the land, along the Nile and its delta.
The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, carries a substantial share of global seaborne trade.
The Great Pyramid of Giza is the only one of the seven ancient wonders still standing.
EG.about: Almost all of Egypt is desert: the Western Desert, dotted with oases such as Siwa and Kharga; the rugged Eastern Desert along the Red Sea; and the Sinai Peninsula, which links Africa to Asia. Rain is rare outside a narrow Mediterranean strip, so the Nile has always been the country's lifeline. Since 1970 the Aswan High Dam has controlled its annual flood, creating Lake Nasser and enabling year-round irrigation. A unified kingdom emerged around 3100 BC, and later rulers included Persians, the Greek Ptolemies, Romans, Arab caliphates from the 7th century, the Mamluks and the Ottomans. Britain occupied the country in 1882 and recognised its independence in 1922, though British influence lasted decades longer; the 1952 revolution led to a republic the following year. Cairo is the largest city in the Arab world, and Egyptian film, music and television have long been influential across Arabic-speaking countries. Tourism, agriculture and natural gas are major parts of the economy.

facts: Equatorial Guinea is the only sovereign African state where Spanish is an official language.
Its capital, Malabo, sits on the island of Bioko rather than the mainland.
Oil discoveries in the 1990s transformed it into one of Africa's largest per-capita oil producers.
GQ.about: Equatorial Guinea is split between a rectangular mainland territory, Río Muni, wedged between Cameroon and Gabon, and several islands in the Gulf of Guinea: volcanic Bioko in the north and tiny Annobón, more than 500 kilometres to the south-west. Hot, humid equatorial weather sustains dense rainforest across most of the mainland. Portugal ceded its claims in the region to Spain in 1778, and Spanish Guinea gained independence on 12 October 1968. The first decade of independence brought harsh repression, and many people fled abroad. The Fang are the majority on the mainland, while the Bubi are the indigenous people of Bioko, and French and Portuguese are also official languages alongside Spanish. Although hydrocarbon revenues raised national income sharply, much of the population has seen limited benefit, and the economy remains heavily dependent on oil and gas. Bioko's southern forests are known for their populations of rare primates.

facts: Asmara's early-20th-century modernist architecture earned the city World Heritage status.
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993 after a thirty-year war.
Its independence left Ethiopia landlocked, redrawing the region's trade routes.
ER.about: A long Red Sea coastline, together with the more than 100 islands of the Dahlak Archipelago, gives Eritrea a strong maritime orientation, with ports at Massawa and Assab. Inland the land climbs to a cool central highland plateau where most people live and farm, and then falls away in the south-east to the Danakil Depression, one of the hottest and lowest places on Earth. Italy made Eritrea a colony in 1890, and Italian investment built railways, roads and towns. British administration followed in 1941, and in 1952 the territory was federated with Ethiopia, which annexed it outright in 1962. After formal independence, a border war with Ethiopia was fought from 1998 to 2000. The state officially recognises nine ethnic groups, of which the Tigrinya and Tigre are the largest, and the population is roughly divided between Christians and Muslims. Most people depend on subsistence farming and herding.

facts: Eswatini is one of the last absolute monarchies in the world.
It changed its name from Swaziland in 2018 to avoid confusion with Switzerland.
The country has two capitals: Mbabane is administrative and Lobamba is legislative and royal.
SZ.about: Though small, Eswatini drops in a series of steps from west to east: the cool, grassy highveld, the farmed middleveld, the hot, dry lowveld, and finally the Lubombo plateau along the border with Mozambique. Several rivers cut through these zones on their way to the Indian Ocean, providing water for irrigated sugar cane estates in the lowveld, the backbone of agricultural exports. The Swazi kingdom took shape in the 19th century, and its name comes from King Mswati II. Britain administered it as a protectorate after the South African War, and independence followed on 6 September 1968. Royal ceremonies such as Umhlanga, the reed dance, and Incwala, the kingship festival, remain central to national life. SiSwati is spoken by almost everyone, giving the country an unusually homogeneous culture. Its economy is closely tied to South Africa, through a customs union and a currency pegged to the rand, and many Swazis work across the border.

facts: Ethiopia was never colonised, apart from a brief Italian occupation from 1936 to 1941.
It uses its own calendar with thirteen months and runs roughly seven to eight years behind the Gregorian one.
Coffee originates here, and the Ethiopian highlands remain a centre of arabica cultivation.
ET.about: Ethiopia's high central plateau, much of it above 2,000 metres, is split diagonally by the Great Rift Valley and drops to hot lowlands on every side. From Lake Tana in the north-west the Blue Nile flows out to supply most of the water reaching Egypt, and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam now harnesses it for electricity. The jagged Simien Mountains and the volcanic Danakil Depression lie at opposite extremes of its relief. The kingdom of Aksum, centred in the north, adopted Christianity in the 4th century, and the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela date from around the 12th and 13th centuries. Ethiopian forces defeated an Italian army at Adwa in 1896. The fossil skeleton known as Lucy, about 3.2 million years old, was found in the Afar region in 1974. It is the second most populous country in Africa, with more than 80 ethnic groups, and Addis Ababa hosts the African Union.

facts: Around 88% of Gabon is forest, and 11% of its territory is protected national park.
Oil wealth gives it one of the higher per-capita incomes in sub-Saharan Africa.
The Oklo uranium deposit hosted a natural nuclear fission reaction around two billion years ago.
GA.about: Straddling the Equator on Africa's Atlantic coast, Gabon is drained almost entirely by the Ogooué River and its tributaries, which flow from the interior plateaus to a broad delta of lagoons and wetlands around Port-Gentil. The landscape is mostly low hills and plateaus under dense rainforest, with savanna patches in the south-east. Libreville was founded in 1849 as a settlement for freed captives from a slave ship, and its name reflects that origin. France incorporated the territory into French Equatorial Africa, and it gained independence on 17 August 1960. At Lambaréné on the Ogooué, Albert Schweitzer founded a hospital in 1913 that made the town known worldwide. Gabon is unusually urbanised for the region, with most people living in Libreville, Port-Gentil and Franceville. Besides oil, it is one of the world's leading producers of manganese. Lopé National Park, combining forest, savanna and ancient rock carvings, is a World Heritage Site.

facts: The Gambia is the smallest country on mainland Africa, a narrow strip along its river.
It is surrounded by Senegal on three sides, with the Atlantic on the fourth.
Its borders roughly follow the navigable stretch of the Gambia River.
GM.about: Mangrove creeks, mudflats and salt-tolerant forest line the lower course of the Gambia River, where seawater pushes far upstream in the dry season. Further inland, the floodplains give way to savanna farmland planted with groundnuts, rice and millet. Kunta Kinteh Island, formerly James Island, was a contested trading fort in the colonial era and is now a World Heritage Site. Britain founded Bathurst, renamed Banjul in 1973, on an island at the river mouth in 1816. The Gambia became independent on 18 February 1965 and a republic in 1970, and between 1982 and 1989 it formed the Senegambia Confederation with Senegal. The Mandinka are the largest ethnic group, alongside the Fula, Wolof, Jola and others, and English is the official language. Groundnuts were long the leading export, and beach tourism along the short Atlantic coast, especially from northern Europe in winter, is an important source of income.

facts: Ghana was the first sub-Saharan African country to gain independence from colonial rule, in 1957.
Lake Volta is among the largest reservoirs in the world by surface area.
It is a leading cocoa producer and was known as the Gold Coast for its mineral wealth.
GH.about: From a low coastal plain dotted with lagoons, Ghana rises to forested hills in the south-west and the broad Volta basin in the centre, before flattening into dry savanna in the north. The Akosombo Dam, completed in 1965, supplies much of the country's electricity. Portuguese traders built Elmina Castle in 1482, and later European powers lined the coast with forts used in the gold and slave trades; many are now World Heritage Sites. Inland, the Asante kingdom, centred on Kumasi, became a powerful state before Britain conquered it around 1900. The name Ghana was taken from a medieval West African empire that lay far to the north-west. Under Kwame Nkrumah the country became a leading voice for pan-Africanism. Gold remains a key export, and offshore oil has been produced since 2010. English is official, while Akan languages such as Twi are widely spoken, and kente cloth is a national emblem.

facts: Guinea holds the world's largest reserves of bauxite, the ore from which aluminium is made.
The Niger, Senegal and Gambia rivers all rise in the Guinea Highlands.
It was the only French colony to reject de Gaulle's 1958 community proposal and take immediate independence.
GN.about: Guinea is often described in four natural regions: the humid coastal plain of Lower Guinea, the sandstone plateaus of the Fouta Djallon in Middle Guinea, the savanna of Upper Guinea and the rainforest-covered highlands of Forest Guinea in the south-east. The coast is one of the wettest in West Africa, with heavy monsoon rains between June and October. In the 18th century Fula Muslims established an Islamic state in the Fouta Djallon, and in the late 19th century Samori Touré resisted French conquest for years. After independence in 1958, Ahmed Sékou Touré ruled until his death in 1984, pursuing a largely isolated socialist path. The Fula, Malinké and Susu are the largest groups. Mount Nimba Strict Nature Reserve, shared with Côte d'Ivoire, is a World Heritage Site, and the country has large deposits of iron ore and gold as well as bauxite.

facts: Guinea-Bissau includes the Bijagós archipelago of around 88 islands, most of them uninhabited.
Cashew nuts dominate its exports and much of its rural economy.
Portuguese is official, but Guinea-Bissau Creole is the common everyday language.
GW.about: Much of Guinea-Bissau is low and flat, cut by broad tidal estuaries such as those of the Cacheu, Geba and Corubal rivers, and fringed with mangroves that make the coastline highly indented. The Balanta and other coastal peoples cultivate rice in reclaimed mangrove swamps, while the interior rises gently to savanna. Portuguese traders were active here from the 15th century, and Cacheu became one of their earliest trading posts in West Africa. The PAIGC liberation movement, founded by Amílcar Cabral, began an armed struggle in 1963 and declared independence on 24 September 1973; Portugal recognised it in 1974 after its own revolution. Since then the country has experienced repeated coups and political instability. The population includes many ethnic groups, among them the Balanta, Fula, Mandinka, Manjaco and Papel. Most people live by farming and fishing, and the tropical climate brings a single rainy season from about June to October.

facts: Ivory Coast is the world's largest cocoa producer, supplying roughly 40% of global output.
The capital moved to Yamoussoukro in 1983, though Abidjan remains the economic centre.
The Basilica of Our Lady of Peace in Yamoussoukro is among the largest church buildings in the world.
CI.about: A chain of lagoons, including the Ébrié lagoon on which Abidjan is built, runs behind the sandy coast of south-eastern Ivory Coast, while the south-west has rockier shores. Inland, tropical rainforest gives way northwards to savanna, and Taï National Park in the west protects one of the last large areas of primary forest in West Africa, where chimpanzees have been observed using stones as tools. France made the territory a colony in 1893, and it became independent on 7 August 1960 under Félix Houphouët-Boigny, who led it until his death in 1993. Rapid growth based on coffee and cocoa in the 1960s and 1970s became known as the 'Ivorian miracle'. Political crises later led to civil conflict in 2002–2007 and 2010–2011. More than 60 ethnic groups live here, alongside large communities from Burkina Faso and Mali, and the government asks that the country be called Côte d'Ivoire in all languages.

facts: The Great Rift Valley runs the length of Kenya and is dotted with soda lakes drawing millions of flamingos.
Kenya pioneered mobile money with M-Pesa, which reshaped banking across East Africa.
Its highland athletes have dominated middle- and long-distance running for decades.
KE.about: Kenya straddles the Equator, rising from a palm-fringed Indian Ocean coast through dry plains to cool central highlands, while much of the north is arid scrubland around Lake Turkana, the world's largest permanent desert lake. On the coast, Swahili trading towns such as Mombasa and Lamu reflect centuries of contact with Arabia and the wider Indian Ocean; Lamu Old Town is a World Heritage Site. Britain declared a protectorate in 1895 and a colony in 1920, encouraging European settlement in the fertile highlands. The Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s preceded independence on 12 December 1963. Swahili and English are both official languages. Tea, cut flowers and coffee are important exports, and wildlife tourism draws visitors to reserves such as the Maasai Mara, where the annual wildebeest migration crosses from Tanzania. Nairobi hosts the global headquarters of the United Nations Environment Programme.

facts: Lesotho is one of only three countries entirely surrounded by a single other country.
It is the only country in the world with all its land above 1,000 metres.
It exports water to South Africa through the Lesotho Highlands Water Project.
LS.about: Mountains cover most of Lesotho, with the Maloti range in the interior and the Drakensberg escarpment along the eastern border. The Senqu, known downstream as the Orange River, rises here, and winters bring frost and snow to the highlands, enough to support a small ski resort. The nation took shape in the 1820s under Moshoeshoe I, who gathered refugees from regional warfare at the flat-topped mountain stronghold of Thaba Bosiu. Pressure from Boer settlers led him to seek British protection in 1868, and the territory became Basutoland. Independence came on 4 October 1966 under a constitutional monarchy. Almost everyone is Basotho and speaks Sesotho, and the conical mokorotlo hat and woollen Basotho blanket are national symbols. Most people live in the western lowlands, and wool, mohair, clothing manufacturing and wages earned in South Africa, historically in its mines, are central to the economy.

facts: Liberia was founded in the 1820s as a settlement for freed African Americans and declared independence in 1847.
Its capital, Monrovia, is named after US President James Monroe.
It operates one of the world's largest ship registries, so a large share of global tonnage flies its flag.
LR.about: Heavy Atlantic rainfall defines Liberia’s geography. Rains from roughly May to October drench a coast of lagoons, mangrove swamps and sandbars, behind which rolling hills climb towards a plateau along the Guinean frontier. Much of the country is still forested, and it holds a large share of what survives of the Upper Guinean rainforest, home to pygmy hippos and forest elephants. Rivers such as the St Paul and Cavalla run roughly parallel towards the sea. Liberia was never colonised by a European power, but for more than a century politics was dominated by the Americo-Liberian minority descended from the settlers, while the indigenous majority, including Kpelle, Bassa and Grebo peoples, had little say. A coup in 1980 ended that order and was followed by two civil wars between 1989 and 2003. Iron ore, timber and rubber, notably from the vast Firestone plantation at Harbel, remain economic mainstays.

facts: Libya is over 90% desert and has the largest proven oil reserves in Africa.
The Great Man-Made River pumps fossil groundwater from beneath the Sahara to the coastal cities.
Leptis Magna is among the best-preserved Roman cities anywhere in the world.
LY.about: Historically this was three regions rather than one: Tripolitania in the north-west; Cyrenaica in the east, whose Jebel Akhdar uplands catch enough rain for woodland and farming; and Fezzan, the desert south, where oases such as Sabha and Murzuq grew along caravan routes. Greek colonists founded Cyrene in the east in the seventh century BC, while the west fell within Carthaginian and then Roman Africa. Italy seized the territory from the Ottoman Empire in 1911–12, and after wartime British and French administration Libya became independent in 1951 as a kingdom under King Idris, through a process overseen by the United Nations. Muammar Gaddafi took power in a 1969 coup and ruled until the 2011 uprising, after which rival authorities in the east and west have competed for control. The country has no permanent rivers, only wadis that flow briefly after rare storms, and the great majority of Libyans live along the Mediterranean coastal strip.

facts: Madagascar is the fourth largest island in the world and separated from other landmasses around 88 million years ago.
Roughly 90% of its wildlife exists nowhere else, including all of the world's lemur species.
Malagasy belongs to the Austronesian family, most closely related to languages of Borneo rather than Africa.
MG.about: A steep escarpment divides Madagascar lengthwise. The central highlands, around 1,200 to 1,500 metres high in many places, drop abruptly to a narrow, rain-soaked eastern coast exposed to the trade winds and to frequent cyclones, and slope more gently to broad western plains of dry forest and savanna, where the island’s distinctive baobabs grow. The far south-west is semi-arid, covered in spiny forest of cactus-like plants. People arrived relatively late, probably within the last two thousand years: seafarers from South-east Asia, later joined by Bantu-speaking Africans, and both heritages shape Malagasy culture. In the 19th century the Merina kingdom of the highlands unified much of the island before France annexed it in 1896; independence followed in 1960. Most Malagasy are farmers, and terraced rice paddies are characteristic of the highlands, while vanilla, of which Madagascar is the world’s leading producer, is a key export. Forest clearance and severe soil erosion, visible in red-scarred hillsides, are serious long-term problems.

facts: Lake Malawi covers about a fifth of the country and holds more fish species than any other lake on Earth.
Malawi is landlocked and one of the most densely populated countries in southern Africa.
It is often called the Warm Heart of Africa, a nickname tied to its tourism image.
MW.about: The East African Rift runs the full length of Malawi, a long, narrow country stretching nearly 900 kilometres from north to south. The rift floor holds the lake and, below it, the Shire River, which drains the lake southwards to join the Zambezi in Mozambique. Highlands rise on either side, including the Nyika Plateau in the north, with its rolling montane grassland, and the granite massif of Mulanje in the south. Scottish missions were established in the region in the 1870s, following David Livingstone’s travels, and Britain declared a protectorate in 1891, later named Nyasaland. It was joined to the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland from 1953 to 1963 and became independent as Malawi in 1964 under Hastings Banda, who ruled as president for life until multi-party elections in 1994. The economy rests on smallholder farming: maize is the staple food and tobacco the leading export. Blantyre, named after Livingstone’s Scottish birthplace, remains the commercial centre.

facts: Timbuktu was a centre of Islamic scholarship, with manuscript libraries dating from the 13th century onward.
The medieval Mali Empire controlled much of the trans-Saharan gold trade.
The Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest mud-brick building in the world and is replastered each year by the town.
ML.about: The Niger River gives Mali its shape and much of its livelihood. Flowing north-east from the Guinea highlands, it spreads across the Inner Niger Delta, a vast seasonal floodplain of channels and lakes that swells after the rains and supports fishing, rice farming and herding, before bending south-east towards Niger. North of the river the land passes through the dry Sahel into the Sahara. Mali takes its name from the medieval empire, but its modern borders were drawn within French West Africa, when it was known as French Sudan. It became independent in 1960, briefly in a federation with Senegal that broke apart within months. Most Malians live in the wetter south and along the river, and the population includes Bambara, Fulani, Songhai, Tuareg and Dogon peoples; the Dogon are known for cliff villages on the Bandiagara Escarpment. Gold and cotton are the main exports, and since 2012 the north and centre have suffered persistent conflict.

facts: Around three quarters of Mauritania is desert, and the Sahara continues to expand southward.
The Richat Structure, a huge circular formation in the desert, is a landmark for astronauts in orbit.
Its coastal waters are among the richest fishing grounds in West Africa.
MR.about: Mauritania forms a bridge between the Arab-Berber Maghreb and sub-Saharan West Africa, and that dual identity runs through its society. Its only permanent river, the Senegal, marks the southern border, and the narrow farming belt along its banks is home to Pulaar-, Soninke- and Wolof-speaking communities, while the north was traditionally home to Arabic-speaking Moorish camel herders. The interior is a sweep of dunes, gravel plains and sandstone plateaus such as the Adrar, where old caravan towns like Chinguetti and Ouadane preserve libraries of Islamic manuscripts. France governed the territory as part of French West Africa, and it became independent in 1960 as an Islamic republic. Severe droughts in the 1970s and 1980s drove many herders into towns, and Nouakchott, built almost from scratch as the capital around independence, now holds a large share of the population. Iron ore from Zouérat, hauled to the coast by some of the world’s longest trains, is a leading export.

highest.name: Piton de la Petite Rivière Noire

facts: The dodo was endemic to Mauritius and was driven extinct within a century of European arrival.
The island was uninhabited before Dutch settlement in the 17th century.
It has one of Africa's highest per-capita incomes, built on tourism, textiles and financial services.
MU.about: Volcanic Mauritius rises to a central plateau ringed by jagged peaks and is almost entirely encircled by a coral reef enclosing calm lagoons. The south-east trade winds make the uplands and windward side far wetter than the sheltered west coast, and tropical cyclones are a seasonal threat. After the Dutch left in 1710, France ruled the island as Île de France and brought enslaved people from Africa and Madagascar to work sugar plantations; Britain captured it in 1810 during the Napoleonic Wars. After slavery was abolished, Britain brought in hundreds of thousands of indentured labourers from India, whose descendants now form the majority. Independence came in 1968, and Mauritius became a republic in 1992. Hindu, Muslim, Christian and Chinese communities live side by side, and Mauritian Creole is the everyday language of most people. Sugar cane still covers much of the farmland, and the state also includes Rodrigues and other outer islands.

facts: Morocco has both Atlantic and Mediterranean coastlines, separated by the Strait of Gibraltar.
The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded in 859, is often cited as the oldest continuously operating university.
The Atlas Mountains shield the fertile north from the Sahara to the south.
MA.about: One of the world’s oldest reigning dynasties, the Alaouites, has ruled Morocco since the 17th century, and earlier dynasties such as the Almoravids and Almohads built empires reaching into Spain. Unlike its neighbours, the country never came under Ottoman rule. In 1912 it was divided into French and Spanish protectorates, with Tangier later placed under international administration, and it regained independence in 1956. Mountains dominate the land: the Rif curves along the Mediterranean, while the Middle, High and Anti-Atlas run broadly south-west to north-east, beyond which date-palm oases and pre-Saharan valleys lead into desert. Amazigh (Berber) heritage is strong, and Tamazight became an official language alongside Arabic in 2011. Most people live on the Atlantic plains and plateaus between Tangier and Agadir, where Casablanca is the economic capital. Phosphates, of which Morocco holds the world’s largest reserves, tourism, farming and car manufacturing drive the economy. The status of Western Sahara, which Morocco administers in large part, remains internationally disputed.

facts: Mozambique has one of Africa's longest coastlines, stretching about 2,500 kilometres on the Indian Ocean.
Its flag is the only national flag to feature a modern rifle.
It joined the Commonwealth in 1995 without ever having been a British colony.
MZ.about: The Zambezi divides Mozambique into two contrasting halves. North of the river the land rises from the coast towards plateaus and highlands near Lake Malawi, while the south is largely low-lying coastal plain, crossed by rivers such as the Limpopo and Save that are prone to severe flooding, and cyclones from the Mozambique Channel strike regularly. Arab and Swahili traders were active on this coast long before Vasco da Gama arrived in 1498, and the Portuguese gradually built a colony around ports such as Ilha de Moçambique, which served as the capital for centuries. Independence in 1975 followed a ten-year liberation war led by FRELIMO and was soon overshadowed by a civil war with RENAMO that lasted until 1992. The Cahora Bassa dam on the Zambezi exports much of its electricity to South Africa. Large offshore natural gas fields have been found in the far north, where an insurgency in Cabo Delgado province has disrupted development since 2017.

facts: The Namib is considered the oldest desert in the world, arid for at least 55 million years.
Namibia was the first country to write environmental protection into its constitution.
The Caprivi Strip, a narrow eastward finger, was drawn to give German colonists access to the Zambezi.
NA.about: Few countries are as thinly populated as Namibia. The cold Benguela Current flows up the Atlantic coast, chilling the air so that rain rarely falls and fog drifts in instead, sustaining beetles, lichens and the long-lived welwitschia plant. Inland, an escarpment climbs to a central plateau of thornbush savanna, the Kalahari stretches east, and only the far north, where most people live, receives regular summer rain. The perennial rivers all lie on the borders: the Orange in the south and the Kunene, Okavango and Zambezi in the north. Germany colonised the territory as German South West Africa in 1884, and its campaign against the Herero and Nama peoples between 1904 and 1908 is widely recognised as genocide. South Africa then ruled it for seven decades and extended apartheid there, until a long liberation struggle led by SWAPO brought independence in 1990. Diamonds, uranium and tourism underpin the economy, and German is still spoken in some towns.

facts: More than 80% of Niger is Sahara, and it is one of the hottest countries on Earth.
It has among the highest birth rates in the world, giving it a very young population.
The Air and Ténéré reserve is one of the largest protected areas in Africa.
NE.about: The Niger River crosses only the far south-west of the country that takes its name, yet that short stretch around Niamey is vital for irrigation and fishing. Most Nigeriens live in a narrow band of Sahelian farmland along the southern border, where millet and sorghum depend on a brief summer rainy season. Further north rise the Aïr Mountains and the dune seas of the Ténéré, crossed for centuries by Tuareg salt caravans bound for the oasis of Bilma. Lake Chad once reached well into the far south-east, but it has shrunk sharply since the 1960s. The territory was part of French West Africa and became independent in 1960. Hausa is the most widely spoken language, and Zinder was once the seat of the Sultanate of Damagaram. Uranium, mined near Arlit since the early 1970s, has long been a leading export, while recurrent drought and food insecurity remain persistent challenges.

facts: Nigeria is the most populous country in Africa, with more people than any European nation.
Nollywood produces more films per year than almost any other film industry in the world.
The capital moved from Lagos to the purpose-built city of Abuja in 1991.
NG.about: Two great rivers shape Nigeria’s map: the Niger, entering from the north-west, and the Benue, flowing in from the east, meet at Lokoja to form a Y that loosely divides the country into its three largest cultural regions. The Hausa-Fulani north is mainly Muslim and lies in dry savanna and Sahel, while the Yoruba south-west and the Igbo south-east are largely Christian; altogether the country has more than 250 ethnic groups. Earlier states included the Sokoto Caliphate, the Oyo Empire and the Kingdom of Benin, famed for its bronze castings. Britain merged its northern and southern protectorates in 1914, and Nigeria became independent in 1960. The Biafran war of 1967–70 followed a secession attempt in the south-east. The Niger Delta, one of the world’s largest wetlands and mangrove systems, holds the oil that has dominated government revenue and exports since the 1970s. Lagos, on a lagoon-fringed coast, is the main commercial hub.

facts: Rwanda is known as the land of a thousand hills for its steep, terraced landscape.
It banned single-use plastic bags in 2008, well ahead of most of the world.
Volcanoes National Park protects a substantial share of the remaining mountain gorillas.
RW.about: Perched on the divide between the Nile and Congo basins, Rwanda lies almost entirely above 1,000 metres, which gives it a mild climate despite sitting just south of the equator. The west drops steeply to Lake Kivu on the floor of the Albertine Rift, the Virunga volcanoes line the north-west border, and the east flattens into savanna, lakes and the papyrus swamps of Akagera National Park. Nyungwe forest in the south-west is one of the largest surviving montane rainforests in East Africa, and streams there are often cited as the most distant source of the Nile. Rwanda was a centralised kingdom long before Germany and then Belgium ruled it, and colonial administrators hardened distinctions between Hutu and Tutsi. After independence in 1962 these divisions culminated in the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi, in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed in about a hundred days. Most Rwandans farm small plots, and coffee and tea are leading exports.

facts: São Tomé and Príncipe is the second smallest African country and sits almost on the equator.
The islands were uninhabited before Portuguese arrival in the 1470s.
Once the world's largest cocoa producer, it still relies heavily on the crop.
ST.about: Both main islands are the summits of extinct volcanoes on the Cameroon Line, a chain of volcanic peaks running from mainland Cameroon south-west into the Gulf of Guinea. Their steep interiors are cloaked in rainforest and cut by deep valleys, and southern São Tomé is studded with volcanic plugs such as the needle-like Pico Cão Grande. Príncipe, much smaller and lying to the north-east, is a UNESCO biosphere reserve. The Portuguese turned the islands into an early centre of plantation sugar worked by enslaved Africans, and later a transit point in the slave trade. Coffee and cocoa estates known as roças followed in the 19th century, relying on contract labourers from Angola, Mozambique and Cape Verde. Independence came in 1975, after Portugal’s revolution of the previous year. Most people live on São Tomé, and Portuguese-based creoles are spoken alongside Portuguese.

facts: Senegal almost completely surrounds The Gambia, which follows its river inland.
Dakar sits on the Cap-Vert peninsula, the westernmost point of mainland Africa.
Gorée Island off Dakar is a memorial to the Atlantic slave trade.
SN.about: Low plains cover most of Senegal, rising only in the south-east where the foothills of the Fouta Djallon begin. The Senegal River forms the northern border and supports irrigated rice and floodplain farming, while in the south the Casamance region, cut off from the rest of the country by The Gambia, is green and forested, with mangrove-lined creeks. Between them, the Sahelian north gives way to the groundnut basin of the centre, long the heart of the export economy. Saint-Louis, at the mouth of the Senegal River, was among France’s earliest settlements in West Africa and served as capital of French West Africa before Dakar replaced it. Senegal became independent in 1960, briefly as part of the Mali Federation, with the poet Léopold Sédar Senghor as its first president. Wolof is the most widely spoken language, Sufi brotherhoods such as the Mourides are deeply influential, and fishing, phosphates and new offshore oil and gas are important.

facts: Seychelles is the smallest African country by both population and land area.
Its inner islands are granite rather than coral or volcanic, a rarity for mid-ocean islands.
The coco de mer palm, found only here, produces the largest seed of any plant.
SC.about: Scattered across a vast stretch of the western Indian Ocean, Seychelles comprises about 115 islands. Most people live on Mahé, with smaller communities on Praslin and La Digue, while the outer islands are low coral atolls and sand cays. Among them is Aldabra, one of the world’s largest raised coral atolls, home to roughly 100,000 giant tortoises. Lying largely outside the cyclone belt, the islands have a warm, humid climate year-round, shaped by alternating monsoon winds. No one lived here until the French founded a settlement in 1770, bringing enslaved Africans to work plantations; Britain took control during the Napoleonic Wars and formally acquired the islands in 1814. Independence followed in 1976. Most Seychellois have mixed African, European and Asian ancestry, and the French-based creole is the main spoken language alongside English and French. Tourism and tuna fishing and processing dominate the economy, and around half of the land area is set aside in protected areas.

facts: Freetown was founded in 1787 as a settlement for freed slaves from Britain, Nova Scotia and Jamaica.
Its natural harbour is among the largest in the world.
Sierra Leone's diamond fields funded the civil war of the 1990s, giving rise to the term blood diamonds.
SL.about: Behind Freetown’s mountainous peninsula, a rare stretch of high ground on this part of the West African coast, Sierra Leone falls into broad bands: a coastal belt of mangrove swamps, creeks and beaches; interior plains of farmland and bush; and a plateau in the north and east rising to the Loma Mountains. The name comes from Portuguese navigators of the 15th century, who called the peninsula’s hills the lion mountains. Britain made Freetown a Crown Colony in 1808, using it as a base for the naval squadron that intercepted slave ships, and declared a protectorate over the interior in 1896. Descendants of the freed settlers, the Krio, gave the country its lingua franca, an English-based creole also called Krio. Independence came in 1961. The civil war of 1991–2002 was followed by the Ebola epidemic of 2014–16. Mende and Temne are the largest ethnic groups, and rice is the staple crop.

facts: Somalia has the longest mainland coastline in Africa, at around 3,300 kilometres.
It is one of the most linguistically and ethnically homogeneous countries on the continent.
Somaliland in the north has functioned self-governed since 1991 without international recognition.
SO.about: Shaped like a figure seven around the tip of the Horn of Africa, Somalia faces the Gulf of Aden to the north and the Indian Ocean to the east. The north is rugged, with mountains rising steeply behind a hot coastal plain, while the centre and south are largely flat, semi-arid plateau and plain. The only two permanent rivers, the Jubba and Shabelle, flow in from the Ethiopian highlands and water the farming belt of the south; the Shabelle usually fades into swamps before reaching the ocean. Rainfall is low and erratic, and pastoralism, especially the herding of camels, goats and sheep, has long been central to Somali life. Coastal towns such as Mogadishu, Merca and Barawa were medieval trading ports on Indian Ocean routes. The modern state was created in 1960, when British Somaliland and the Italian-administered south united at independence. After the central government collapsed in 1991, the country endured prolonged conflict and recurrent drought.

facts: South Africa has three capital cities: Pretoria for the executive, Cape Town for parliament and Bloemfontein for the judiciary.
It recognises twelve official languages, among the most of any country.
It completely surrounds Lesotho and produces a large share of the world's platinum.
ZA.about: Much of South Africa is a high interior plateau ringed by the Great Escarpment, whose loftiest section is the Drakensberg in the east. Below it, the coasts differ sharply: the Indian Ocean coast of KwaZulu-Natal is humid and subtropical, the cold Benguela Current keeps the west coast dry, and the south-western Cape has a Mediterranean climate with winter rain and the fynbos of the Cape Floral Kingdom, one of the richest plant regions on Earth. The Dutch founded a station at the Cape in 1652; Britain took over in the early 19th century, and the discovery of diamonds at Kimberley and gold on the Witwatersrand transformed the economy. The Union of South Africa was formed in 1910, and from 1948 the apartheid system enforced racial segregation until negotiations led to the first democratic elections in 1994, which brought Nelson Mandela to the presidency. Johannesburg grew on the gold reefs and anchors one of Africa’s most industrialised economies.

facts: South Sudan became independent in 2011 and is the world's youngest widely recognised country.
The Sudd, a vast wetland on the White Nile, is one of the largest in the world.
It is landlocked and depends on pipelines through Sudan to export its oil.
SS.about: Much of South Sudan is a vast clay plain drained by the White Nile and its tributaries, such as the Bahr el Ghazal and Sobat, which flood widely each rainy season. Higher ground appears in the far south, where the Imatong Mountains rise near the Ugandan border, and in the south-west, where the plain climbs to an ironstone plateau along the Congo–Nile watershed. The floodplain grasslands support one of Africa’s largest mammal migrations, of white-eared kob and other antelope. Cattle are central to the economy and identity of Nilotic peoples such as the Dinka and Nuer, the two largest groups. Under Anglo-Egyptian rule the south was administered largely apart from the north, and two long civil wars, from 1955 to 1972 and from 1983 to 2005, ended with a peace agreement that opened the way to a referendum on secession. A new civil war broke out in 2013. Most people live by farming and herding.

facts: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt, built by the Kingdom of Kush at Meroë.
The Blue and White Niles meet at Khartoum to form the main Nile.
It was Africa's largest country until South Sudan separated in 2011.
SD.about: Sudan runs from near-rainless desert in the north to savanna in the south. The Nile winds through the north in a great S-shaped bend broken by cataracts, flanked by the Nubian Desert, while the Red Sea Hills separate the interior from the coast at Port Sudan. In the west, the volcanic massif of Jebel Marra rises above the plains of Darfur. Between the Blue and White Niles, the Gezira scheme, begun under British rule in the 1920s, became one of the world’s largest irrigation projects, long devoted to cotton. Egypt conquered the region in the 1820s, and the Mahdist uprising of the 1880s overthrew Egyptian rule until an Anglo-Egyptian force retook the country in 1898. Independence came in 1956. Arabic-speaking Muslims form the majority, alongside many other peoples. Conflict has repeatedly shaped modern Sudan, including the war in Darfur from 2003 and the fighting that began in 2023. Gum arabic, livestock and gold are major exports.

facts: Kilimanjaro is the highest point in Africa and the tallest free-standing mountain in the world.
Tanzania borders three of Africa's great lakes: Victoria, Tanganyika and Malawi.
The country was formed in 1964 by the union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar.
TZ.about: The Serengeti plains of northern Tanzania, continuing into Kenya, host the largest overland migration of wildebeest and zebra on Earth, and the neighbouring Ngorongoro Crater, a collapsed volcano, holds one of Africa’s densest concentrations of large mammals. Much of the country is a high central plateau, bounded by rift valleys in the west and descending to a hot, humid coastal plain on the Indian Ocean, where Swahili culture developed through centuries of trade with Arabia, Persia and India; Kilwa Kisiwani was a powerful medieval trading city. Germany colonised the mainland as part of German East Africa, and Britain administered it after the First World War. Tanganyika became independent in 1961 under Julius Nyerere, whose promotion of Swahili as a national language helped bind together more than 120 ethnic groups. Dar es Salaam remains the main port and commercial hub. Agriculture employs most people, while gold mining and tourism earn much of the foreign exchange.

facts: Togo is one of Africa's narrowest countries, roughly 115 kilometres wide but 550 long.
It is among the world's largest producers of phosphate rock.
Koutammakou, in the north, is known for its fortified mud tower-houses.
TG.about: Togo’s Atlantic coast is little more than 50 kilometres long, lined with sandbars and lagoons such as Lake Togo, behind which a plateau rises gradually northwards. The Togo Mountains, part of the Atakora range, cross the country diagonally from south-west to north-east, and beyond them the north is drier savanna drained by the Oti River. Germany established the protectorate of Togoland in 1884; after the First World War it was divided between Britain and France, and the British western part later joined Ghana, leaving the Ewe divided between the two. French Togo became independent in 1960. The ethnic map runs from Ewe and Mina communities in the south to Kabye and other groups in the north. Lomé’s deep-water port is among the busiest in West Africa and a gateway for landlocked neighbours, while cotton, coffee and cocoa are grown for export. Subsistence farming of yams, maize and cassava supports most of the population.

facts: Tunisia is the northernmost country in Africa and the smallest in the Maghreb.
Carthage, near modern Tunis, was Rome's great rival before its destruction in 146 BC.
Parts of the Sahara here have stood in for other planets in numerous films.
TN.about: The eastern end of the Atlas Mountains, known here as the Dorsal, runs across Tunisia from south-west to north-east, dividing a greener, wetter north from the steppe and desert of the south. The north has the country’s only perennial river, the Medjerda, whose fertile valley was once a granary for Rome. Along the eastern coast, the Sahel region around Sousse and Sfax is covered in olive groves, making Tunisia one of the world’s leading olive oil exporters. Further south lie the salt flats of Chott el Djerid and the dunes of the Grand Erg Oriental, while the island of Djerba has an ancient Jewish community. After the Arab conquest in the seventh century, Kairouan became a major centre of Islamic learning. Tunisia was a French protectorate from 1881 to 1956. Under Habib Bourguiba it adopted a progressive personal status code that banned polygamy, and in 2010–11 it was where the Arab Spring began.

facts: Uganda shares Lake Victoria, the largest lake in Africa, with Kenya and Tanzania.
The Nile's most commonly cited source is at Jinja, where it leaves Lake Victoria.
The Rwenzori range, the Mountains of the Moon, carries glaciers despite sitting on the equator.
UG.about: Lying across the equator on a plateau mostly over 1,000 metres high, Uganda has a milder, wetter climate than its latitude might suggest, and much of the south is green and fertile. From Lake Victoria the Victoria Nile flows north through Lake Kyoga and forces its way through a narrow gorge at Murchison Falls before entering Lake Albert, which lies with Lake Edward in the western branch of the Rift Valley. Mount Elgon, an extinct volcano, straddles the Kenyan border in the east, while the north-east is the semi-arid Karamoja region. Before colonial rule, kingdoms such as Buganda, Bunyoro and Toro flourished, and Buganda’s prominence gave the country its name. Britain declared a protectorate in 1894, and independence followed in 1962. The 1970s under Idi Amin brought brutal repression and the expulsion of the Asian community. Coffee is the leading export, and Uganda has one of the youngest populations in the world.

facts: Zambia borders eight countries, more than any other in southern Africa.
Victoria Falls on the Zambezi forms the largest sheet of falling water in the world.
Copper has dominated its economy since the colonial era, and the Copperbelt remains its industrial heart.
ZM.about: Most of Zambia lies on a high plateau of miombo woodland and grassland, broken by the deep troughs of the Luangwa and middle Zambezi valleys. The Zambezi drains most of the country, but the north belongs to the Congo basin through the Chambeshi and Luapula rivers and the Bangweulu wetlands, whose floodplains support great herds of black lechwe antelope. Lake Tanganyika reaches into the far north, and South Luangwa National Park is renowned for its walking safaris. The territory came under the British South Africa Company in the 1890s as Northern Rhodesia, passed to direct British rule in 1924 and was part of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland before independence in 1964 under Kenneth Kaunda, who governed until 1991. Zambia has more than 70 ethnic groups, with Bemba and Nyanja among the most widely spoken languages. Most rural households grow maize, the staple food.

facts: Great Zimbabwe, a stone city built between the 11th and 15th centuries, gave the country its name.
Hyperinflation in 2008 forced the abandonment of the Zimbabwean dollar for nearly a decade.
Lake Kariba on the Zambezi is one of the largest artificial lakes in the world by volume.
ZW.about: Zimbabwe occupies a high plateau between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers. A broad ridge, the Highveld, runs from south-west to north-east across the centre, falling away to the Middleveld and then to the hotter, drier Lowveld of the south and the Zambezi valley in the north. Along the eastern border, the Eastern Highlands are cool, wet and partly forested, while the Matobo Hills near Bulawayo are known for granite outcrops and ancient rock art. Hwange in the west is the largest national park and holds very large elephant herds. Cecil Rhodes’s British South Africa Company occupied the region from 1890, and as Southern Rhodesia it was governed by a white minority that declared independence unilaterally in 1965. After a guerrilla war, internationally recognised independence came in 1980. Shona speakers form the majority and Ndebele the largest minority. Farming, notably of maize and tobacco, and mining of gold, platinum and lithium sustain the economy.
